newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Poisonous Soviet legacy hits health in Kazakhstan.
newsitem.headline: Poisonous Soviet legacy hits health in Kazakhstan.

text.p: Decades of Soviet nuclear tests, industrial pollution and reckless use of toxic fertilisers threaten Kazakhstan with a demographic crisis, health experts said on Friday.

"Kazakhstan is a unique country -- it suffered from all types of environmental pressures in Soviet times," Deputy Health Minister Akan Akanov told reporters following a conference held with the United Nations on reproductive health.
During the Cold War, Soviet officials boasted of Kazakhstan's achievements in nuclear weapons tests, space launches from its rolling steppe and heavy industry which devoured vast local resources.
But since independence in 1991, they have left Kazakhstan with a deadly environmental legacy.
"Nuclear tests, industrial pollution and overuse of fertilisers are major reasons for this troubled situation," Akanov said.

Officials in Kazakhstan, a resource-rich Central Asian state the size of Western Europe with a population of 16.7 million people, are alarmed by rising death rates while life expectancy and birth rates plummet.
Nina Kayupova, head of the presidential commission on family, women and demography, said that average life expectancy fell last year to 64.9 years from 66.3 in 1994.
Average male life expectancy of 59.7 years now falls short of the official retirement age of 60.
She said that birth rates fell last year to 15.2 per 1,000 people from 21.7 per 1,000 in 1990. Death rates rose to 10.0 from 7.7 per 1,000 people over the same period.
"The problem of a small population is acute for Kazakhstan -- we are five times the size of France and have collective farms almost the size of the Netherlands," Kayupova said.
She added that Kazakhstan -- unlike other Asian states -- would welcome a higher birth rate.
But illness among the Kazakh young remains a major problem. Akanov said every child in the north-eastern Semipalatinsk and southern Kyzyl Orda regions suffers from anaemia.
In Soviet times, more than 400 nuclear charges were detonated at test sites around Semipalatinsk.
Kyzyl Orda adjoins the shrinking Aral Sea, which began drying up when the Soviets diverted rivers from the sea to feed an ambitious cotton production plan.
Missile fuel dumped across hundreds of kilometers of weapons testing sites and around the famous Baikonur cosmodrome have caused blood diseases and inborn deformities.
Northern Kazakhstan's smokey industrial belt accounts for the highest rate of cancer among the five Central Asian states, Akanov said.
Pesticides, overused in Soviet times, are also a killer.
"We have regions where pesticides are found in blood of up to 70 percent of the local population," Akanov said.
